entry: British actress. Known for her wit in comedic and dramatic roles, she had an extensive career on stage and screen spanning eight decades. She won two Academy Awards, for *The Prime of Miss Jean Brodie* (1969) and *California Suite* (1978), and a Tony Award for *Lettice and Lovage* (1990). She portrayed Professor Minerva McGonagall in the *Harry Potter* film series and played Violet Crawley in *Downton Abbey*, earning three Primetime Emmy Awards. She was made a dame by [[Elizabeth II]] in 1990.

Region of North Africa, the western part of the Arab world. It comprises [[Algeria]], [[Libya]], [[Mauritania]], [[Morocco]], [[Tunisia]] and the disputed territory of [[Western Sahara]], with over 100 million people as of 2018. Berber and Arab dynasties ruled much of it from the 8th to 13th centuries, and European powers administered most of it in the mid-to-late 19th and early 20th centuries. The Arab Maghreb Union, founded in 1989, is largely dormant because of tensions between Algeria and Morocco over Western Sahara.

American basketball player and businessman. Johnson spent his entire playing career with the [[Los Angeles Lakers]] of the [[National Basketball Association|NBA]], leading the team to five championships during its Showtime era. He won three NBA Most Valuable Player awards and holds the league record for average assists per playoff game, 12.35. After announcing in 1991 that he had contracted HIV, he became an advocate for [[HIV/AIDS]] prevention. He later joined the ownership groups of several sports teams.

Collectible card game first released by Wizards of the Coast in 1993. Created by Richard Garfield, it has players represent dueling wizards called Planeswalkers, who usually win by reducing opponents' life totals to zero, often through combat damage. Constructed formats use decks usually of at least 60 cards, while limited formats use decks of at least 40 cards drawn from random pools. By 2023 the game had about fifty million players worldwide. For the 2022 fiscal year, Hasbro reported that Magic had generated $1 billion in annual revenue.

Performing art that uses tricks and illusions of seemingly impossible feats, achieved by natural means. It is one of the oldest performing arts and is distinguished from supernatural magic, which claims supernatural causes. Entertainment magic was pioneered in the 19th century by Jean-Eugène Robert-Houdin, and in the late 19th and early 20th centuries performers such as [[Harry Houdini]] achieved widespread success during the Golden Age of Magic, when performance magic became a staple of [[Broadway theatre|Broadway]], vaudeville and music halls. Magicians use sleight of hand, misdirection, optical and auditory illusions, hidden compartments and psychological techniques such as suggestion and [[Hypnosis|hypnosis]]. They closely guard their methods but share techniques through training within the magic community. Into the 21st century, magic has adapted to [[Television|television]] and the internet, and social media allows magicians to reach wider audiences than ever before.

Practice of beliefs, rituals or actions intended to manipulate natural or supernatural beings and forces. Sometimes spelled magick, it is a category into which various beliefs and practices have been placed, sometimes considered separate from both religion and science. Since the early 1930s, modern anthropology has held that there is complete continuity between magic and religion, though the separation of the two terms is disputed. Hellenistic authors applied the label to practices such as enchantment, [[Divination|divination]] and [[Astrology|astrology]], and early Christians associated magic with [[Demon|demons]]. In the 19th century, [[Anthropology|anthropologists]] Edward Tylor and James G. Frazer defined magic as belief in hidden sympathies between objects, portraying it as the opposite of [[Science|science]]. Marcel Mauss and Émile Durkheim instead contrasted private magical rites with communal religion. By the 1990s many scholars had rejected the term as a useful category for scholarship.

Rail transport system whose vehicles are levitated by magnets rather than rolled on wheels. Maglev trains can reach higher top speeds than conventional railways and have lower maintenance costs and noise, but they are more expensive to build and cannot use existing infrastructure. The speed record of 603 km/h (375 mph) was set by Japan's experimental L0 Series in 2015. From 2002 until 2021, the fastest operational passenger train was the [[Shanghai]] maglev, which uses German Transrapid technology and runs at 431 km/h (268 mph). Only six maglev trains are operational, four of them in China.

Molten or semi-molten rock beneath the surface of Earth, the source of all [[Igneous rock|igneous rocks]]. It may also contain suspended crystals and gas bubbles. Magma is produced by melting of the mantle or crust in tectonic settings including subduction zones, continental rift zones, mid-ocean ridges and hotspots. It may be stored in a [[Magma chamber|magma chamber]] before it feeds a [[Volcano|volcano]] and erupts as lava, or it may solidify underground as intrusions such as dikes, sills and batholiths. Magmas are classified by silica content as felsic, intermediate, mafic or ultramafic, and silica content correlates with viscosity and temperature. Felsic magmas contain more than 63% silica and are highly viscous, so their lavas usually erupt explosively. Magma has been encountered directly during geothermal drilling only three times, twice in Iceland and once in Hawaii.

Large pool of molten rock beneath the Earth's surface, often beneath [[Volcano|volcanoes]]. Magma rises through cracks because it is less dense than the surrounding rock, and it pools in a chamber when it cannot find a path upward. Chambers are commonly built up over time by successive injections, and most known chambers lie between 1 km and 10 km down. As the magma cools, denser minerals crystallize and sink. Gas released as crystals form can raise chamber pressure, possibly enough to produce an eruption. [[Supervolcano|Supervolcano]] eruptions are possible only when an extraordinarily large chamber forms at a shallow level.

English royal charter of rights, sealed by King John at Runnymede in 1215. Drafted to make peace between John and rebel barons, it promised protection of church rights, protection from illegal imprisonment and swift justice. Neither side kept its commitments, and [[Pope Innocent III]] annulled it, leading to the First Barons' War. Reissued in 1216 and 1225 under Henry III, it was confirmed as part of England's statute law in 1297 under [[Edward I]]. Seventeenth-century jurists such as Sir Edward Coke invoked it against the divine right of kings, and it influenced the [[Thirteen Colonies]]. Victorian historians later showed that the original concerned relations between monarch and barons, not ordinary subjects. Three clauses remain in force in England and Wales through the 1297 version. Four exemplifications of the 1215 charter survive, two at the [[British Library]].

Chemical element with symbol Mg and atomic number 12. Magnesium is a shiny gray metal with low density and high chemical reactivity. It is an [[Alkaline earth metal|alkaline earth metal]] that occurs naturally only in combination with other elements and almost always has an oxidation state of +2. The pure metal burns with a brilliant-white light and is mainly obtained by electrolysis of salts from brine. Less dense than [[Aluminium|aluminum]], it is used mainly in strong, lightweight alloys. Magnesium ranks eighth in abundance in Earth's crust and is the third most abundant dissolved element in seawater. It is required for many core cellular functions and for some 300 [[Enzyme|enzymes]], and magnesium compounds serve as common laxatives and antacids.

White crystalline salt with the formula MgSO₄, soluble in water. It is usually encountered as a hydrate, most commonly the heptahydrate MgSO₄·7H₂O, known as Epsom salt. Its main use is in [[Agriculture|agriculture]], where it corrects soils deficient in magnesium, an essential plant nutrient because of its role in [[Chlorophyll|chlorophyll]] and photosynthesis. Annual production was 2.3 million tons by the mid-1970s and approximately 2.6 million tons in 2024. It is used externally as bath salts and internally as a replacement therapy for magnesium deficiency. Hospitals use it to treat abnormal blood magnesium levels and constipation, and to reduce the risk of seizures in eclampsia. Other potential uses include treatment of severe [[Arrhythmia|arrhythmias]] and as a bronchodilator for [[Asthma|asthma]].

Material or object that produces a magnetic field. Magnets attract ferromagnetic materials such as [[Iron|iron]], steel, nickel and cobalt, and attract or repel other magnets. Permanent magnets keep their field without external energy and are made from hard ferromagnetic materials such as alnico and ferrite, processed in a strong magnetic field during manufacture. Soft materials such as annealed iron can be magnetized but do not tend to stay magnetized. An [[Electromagnet|electromagnet]] is a coil of wire that acts as a magnet only while electric current flows through it, and a soft ferromagnetic core, such as mild steel, greatly enhances its field. Ancient people learned about magnetism from [[Magnetite|lodestone]], naturally magnetized pieces of iron ore, and by the 12th to 13th centuries AD, magnetic [[Compass|compasses]] were used in navigation in China, Europe and elsewhere.

Type of [[Neutron star|neutron star]] with an extremely powerful magnetic field. Their magnetic-field decay powers emission of X-rays and [[Gamma ray|gamma rays]]. The concept was proposed in 1992 by Robert Duncan and Christopher Thompson to explain soft gamma repeaters. Of roughly 3,000 neutron stars, 31 are confirmed magnetars, as of January 2021. They are about 20 km in diameter, and their strong fields decay after about 10,000 years. It has been suggested that magnetars are the source of fast radio bursts.

Physical property of space that quantifies the magnetic influence at a given location. Magnetic fields deflect moving electric charges and currents, apply torques that twist magnets, attract or repel magnets and magnetic materials such as [[Iron|iron]], and induce electric currents in conducting material. They are created by permanent magnetic materials and by moving electric charges, including electric current. Because strength and direction vary with location, the field is a vector field, described by two closely related quantities, B and H. In magnetostatics, the field of a steady current is given by the Biot–Savart law. Magnetic fields are central to [[Electric motor|electric motors]], generators, transformers and electromagnets, and the [[Hall effect]] reveals charge carriers in materials. Earth's magnetic field creates a magnetosphere that shields the planet from the [[Solar wind|solar wind]].

Medical imaging technique that generates pictures of the anatomy and physiological processes inside the body. MRI uses strong magnetic fields, field gradients and radio waves, not X-rays or ionizing radiation, which distinguishes it from [[CT scan|computed tomography]] and positron emission tomography. Because [[Hydrogen|hydrogen]] atoms are abundant in water and fat, most scans essentially map where water and fat are located in the body. Pulses of radio waves excite the nuclear spin of [[Proton|protons]], and gradients localize the signal in space. MRI was developed in the 1970s and 1980s from nuclear magnetic resonance research, and Paul Lauterbur proposed using a magnetic field gradient to create images in a two-dimensional plane. Compared with CT, it gives better contrast for soft tissues, but scans are longer and louder, and metal implants may pose a risk.

Storage medium consisting of a thin magnetizable coating on a long, narrow strip of plastic film. It was developed in Germany in 1928, based on earlier magnetic wire recording from Denmark, and can record and play back audio, video and digital computer data. Magnetic tape allowed radio programs to be recorded for later or repeated airing, and since the early 1950s it has been used with computers for data storage and backup. Tape begins to degrade after 10 to 20 years, so it is not ideal for long-term archiving, although formats such as LTO are designed for that purpose. Other technologies have replaced tape in many roles: hard disk drives for software once stored on [[Cassette tape|cassettes]], CDs for cassette audio, and DVDs for [[VHS]] video. [[Sony]] and [[IBM]] continue to advance tape capacity.

Black iron oxide mineral and one of the main [[Iron ore|iron ores]]. With the chemical formula Fe²⁺(Fe³⁺)₂O₄, it is ferrimagnetic and the most magnetic of all naturally occurring minerals, apart from extremely rare native iron. Naturally magnetized pieces, called lodestone, attract small pieces of iron, which is how ancient peoples first discovered magnetism. It is black with a metallic luster, has a Mohs hardness of 5–6 and leaves a black streak. Small grains are very common in [[Igneous rock|igneous]] and [[Metamorphic rock|metamorphic]] rocks. Its structure was among the first determined by X-ray diffraction, in 1915.

Fictional mutant character in [[Marvel Comics]], associated with the [[X-Men]]. Created by writer Stan Lee and artist Jack Kirby, he first appeared in 1963 as an adversary of the X-Men. His mutant power is the ability to generate and control magnetic fields. Later writers established him as a Holocaust survivor, born Max Eisenhardt, whose extreme methods reflect a determination to protect mutants from persecution. His role evolved from supervillain to antihero and eventually superhero. Ian McKellen and Michael Fassbender have portrayed him in the X-Men film series.

Branch of physics concerned with magnetism in systems with steady electric currents. It is the magnetic analog of [[Electrostatics|electrostatics]], where charges are stationary. Its equations can predict fast magnetic switching events lasting nanoseconds or less, and it is even a good approximation when currents are not steady, provided they do not alternate rapidly. It is widely used in micromagnetics, such as models of computer memory storage devices. Starting from [[Maxwell's equations]] and assuming steady currents, the equations separate into independent sets for the electric and magnetic fields. For a known current distribution, the magnetic field follows from the Biot–Savart law, and it can also be derived from a vector potential. Magnetization in strongly magnetic materials must be included explicitly.

Logarithmic measure of the brightness of an astronomical object. The scale is logarithmic, so a magnitude 1 star is exactly 100 times brighter than a magnitude 6 star, and each step is about 2.512 times brighter than the one above. The brighter an object appears, the lower its magnitude, and the brightest objects have negative values. Apparent magnitude is an object's brightness, which depends on its intrinsic luminosity, distance and extinction. Absolute magnitude is the apparent magnitude an object would have at 10 [[Parsec|parsecs]] for stars. [[Hipparchus]] introduced an imprecise but systematic system of magnitudes in ancient times. The Sun has an apparent magnitude of −27, and [[Sirius]] is −1.46.

Clade of flowering plants with more than 10,000 species. Members include magnolias, nutmeg, bay laurel, cinnamon, [[Avocado|avocado]], [[Black pepper|black pepper]] and tulip trees, and the group is the third-largest of the angiosperms after the [[Eudicots|eudicots]] and monocots. Magnoliids are characterized by trimerous flowers, pollen with one pore and usually branching-veined leaves. Some are among the earliest angiosperms and share anatomical features with [[Gymnosperm|gymnosperms]], such as stamens that resemble the male cone scales of [[Conifer|conifers]]. Molecular clock calculations place the split of their lineage from other plants about 135 million years ago, or 160–165 million years ago.

Norwegian chess grandmaster. He won the classical World Chess Champion title five times, from 2013 until declining to defend it in 2023. He has been the world No. 1 in FIDE rankings since July 1, 2011, and his peak rating of 2882 is the highest since FIDE introduced ratings in 1970. Carlsen earned the grandmaster title at 13. In 2014 he became the first player to hold the World Rapid, World Blitz and classical titles at once. Praised for his endgame play, he uses varied openings to make opponents' preparation harder. He trails only [[Garry Kasparov]] in time spent as the highest-rated player in the world.

One of the two major Sanskrit epics of ancient India, revered in Hinduism. It narrates the dynastic struggle for the throne of Hastinapura, which leads to the battle of Kurukshetra between the Kauravas and the Pandavas. It includes the *Bhagavad Gita* and discusses philosophical concepts such as the four goals of life. Traditionally attributed to [[Vyasa]], it was probably compiled between the 3rd century BCE and the 3rd century CE, reaching its final form by the early Gupta period. At about 1.8 million words, it is roughly ten times the length of the *Iliad* and the *Odyssey* combined. Within the Indian tradition it is sometimes called the fifth Veda.

State in western peninsular India, occupying much of the [[Deccan Plateau]]. It is India's second-most populous state, and its capital, [[Mumbai]], is the country's financial and commercial center. Nagpur serves as the winter capital. The state has the largest economy in India, accounting for 14% of all-India nominal GDP, with services dominating. Early in the 19th century the [[East India Company|British East India Company]] brought most of the region under its control. After Indian independence, a movement for a Marathi-speaking state led to the creation of Maharashtra on May 1, 1960, when the State of Bombay was divided into Maharashtra and [[Gujarat]]. The state has seven UNESCO World Heritage Sites, including the Ajanta Caves and Ellora Caves. Its two major rivers are the Godavari and Krishna.
